name: Michael Johnson
chief_complaint: Severe shortness of breath and leg swelling for 3 days
opening_statement: I can't breathe properly when I lie down, and my legs have swollen up badly over the past few days. I'm really worried because I haven't been this bad before.
emotional_baseline: Anxious and distressed, sitting upright in visible respiratory distress, speaking in short sentences due to dyspnoea

symptoms.name: Dyspnoea
symptoms.character: Severe breathlessness, worse when lying flat (orthopnoea), requiring 3 pillows to sleep
symptoms.timing: Constant, worsening at night with paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (PND) waking patient 2-3 times

rag_citations.content: Acute decompensated heart failure presents with progressive dyspnoea, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, and peripheral oedema

symptoms.name: Peripheral Oedema
symptoms.character: Bilateral pitting oedema extending to mid-shin, worse in evenings

rag_citations.content: Fluid overload in acute heart failure manifests as peripheral oedema, rapid weight gain (>2kg in 3 days), and ascites in severe cases

symptoms.name: Fatigue
symptoms.onset: Chronic, worsened significantly in past week
symptoms.character: Profound tiredness limiting all activities of daily living
associated_symptoms: Reduced exercise tolerance (now limited to 10 metres)

rag_citations.content: Reduced cardiac output in heart failure causes exercise intolerance, fatigue, and reduced functional capacity (NYHA Class III-IV in acute decompensation)

symptoms.name: Productive Cough
symptoms.character: Frequent cough producing pink-tinged frothy sputum
symptoms.timing: Worse at night and when lying down

rag_citations.content: Pulmonary oedema in acute heart failure produces pink frothy sputum, nocturnal cough, and orthopnoea due to alveolar fluid accumulation

past_medical_history.details: Anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI to LAD, 3 stents placed
past_medical_history.current_status: Stable angina (CCS Class II) until this week

rag_citations.content: Ischaemic heart disease is the leading cause of heart failure in Australia, accounting for 60-70% of cases

past_medical_history.details: Baseline eGFR 35-40 mL/min/1.73m², secondary to hypertensive nephrosclerosis

rag_citations.content: Cardiorenal syndrome complicates heart failure management, requiring careful diuretic dosing and monitoring of renal function

past_medical_history.details: Long-standing essential hypertension, previous BP poorly controlled (150-160/90-100 mmHg)
past_medical_history.current_status: Recently improved control (130-140/80-85 mmHg) with medication adjustment 3 months ago

past_medical_history.details: Diet and oral hypoglycaemic controlled, HbA1c 7.2% (55 mmol/mol) at last check 6 weeks ago
past_medical_history.current_status: Stable, no recent hypoglycaemia or complications

medications.name: Metoprolol
medications.compliance: Good, but sometimes skips evening dose if feeling dizzy

medications.name: Frusemide
medications.indication: Fluid management in chronic heart failure
medications.compliance: Good, but hasn't increased dose despite worsening symptoms

medications.name: GTN Spray
medications.compliance: Uses occasionally, last used 4 days ago for chest discomfort

allergies: NKDA (No Known Drug Allergies). Patient reports mild gastrointestinal upset with NSAIDs in the past (not a true allergy).
family_history: Father died aged 68 from myocardial infarction. Mother had hypertension and died aged 82 from stroke. Younger brother (aged 72) has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. No family history of sudden cardiac death or inherited cardiomyopathies.

social_history.occupation: Retired postal worker (retired 11 years ago at age 65)
social_history.living_situation: Lives with wife in single-storey home, has 2 adult children living nearby who help with shopping
social_history.smoking: Ex-smoker, quit 20 years ago (2006), previously 20 cigarettes/day for 35 years (35 pack-years)
social_history.alcohol: Occasional social drinker, 1-2 standard drinks per week, no recent increase
social_history.exercise: Previously walked 30 minutes daily, now limited to walking around the house due to dyspnoea
social_history.diet: Generally healthy, wife cooks meals, admits to eating processed foods 2-3 times per week, high salt intake likely
social_history.functional_status: Independent in ADLs until this week, now requires assistance with showering and dressing, uses walking stick for stability

vital_signs.blood_pressure: 160/95 mmHg (elevated due to fluid overload and anxiety)
vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: 88% on room air, improves to 94% on 4L/min oxygen via nasal prongs

examination_findings.general: Patient appears unwell, anxious, sitting upright in tripod position, unable to complete full sentences without pausing for breath

cardiovascular.jvp: Elevated at 8cm above sternal angle (significant venous congestion)
cardiovascular.heart_sounds: Irregularly irregular rhythm, S3 gallop present (volume overload), no murmurs appreciated
cardiovascular.peripheral_pulses: Palpable but weak peripherally, cool extremities suggesting reduced perfusion
cardiovascular.oedema: Bilateral pitting oedema to mid-shin (2+ pitting), sacral oedema present

respiratory.inspection: Increased work of breathing, use of accessory muscles
respiratory.percussion: Dull at both lung bases (pleural effusions)
respiratory.auscultation: Bibasal fine crackles extending to mid-zones, mild expiratory wheeze (cardiac asthma)

abdominal.palpation: Tender hepatomegaly (liver edge 4cm below costal margin), mild ascites

examination_findings.neurological: Alert and oriented, no focal neurological deficits, mild confusion (likely hypoxia-related)

required.expected_findings: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response (rate 110-120 bpm), left ventricular hypertrophy, old anterior Q waves (previous STEMI), no acute ST changes
Cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio >0.55), bilateral pulmonary oedema (bat-wing appearance), bilateral pleural effusions, upper lobe blood diversion (Kerley B lines)
Mildly elevated (0.08 ng/mL, reference <0.04) - likely demand ischaemia, not acute MI
Significantly elevated (>3000 pg/mL, reference <125) confirming acute decompensated heart failure
Mild anaemia (Hb 110 g/L) contributing to decompensation, WCC normal (no infection)
Acute on chronic renal impairment (Cr 180 μmol/L, baseline 150 μmol/L), eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73m² (down from baseline 38), hypernatraemia 148 mmol/L (fluid restriction attempt)
Severe LV systolic dysfunction (LVEF 25-30%, down from 40% 6 months ago), moderate mitral regurgitation (functional), dilated left atrium, elevated pulmonary artery pressures (PASP 55 mmHg)

expected_diagnosis: Acute Decompensated Heart Failure (ADHF) with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), precipitated by new-onset atrial fibrillation and medication non-compliance. NYHA Class IV. Cardiorenal syndrome Type 1.

expected_management.action: Admit to hospital for intravenous diuretic therapy and monitoring
expected_management.rationale: Patient is in acute pulmonary oedema with hypoxia requiring urgent treatment

rag_citation.content: Acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema requires hospital admission for IV diuretics, oxygen therapy, and haemodynamic monitoring

expected_management.action: Oxygen therapy via nasal prongs targeting SpO2 92-96%
expected_management.rationale: Correct hypoxia while avoiding hyperoxia in cardiac patients

rag_citation.content: Supplemental oxygen should be administered to maintain SpO2 92-96% in acute heart failure with hypoxia

expected_management.action: IV frusemide 80mg stat, then 40mg IV BD (double oral dose given acute decompensation)
expected_management.rationale: Achieve rapid diuresis to reduce pulmonary congestion

rag_citation.content: IV loop diuretics at 2-2.5 times the oral dose are first-line for acute decompensated heart failure with fluid overload

expected_management.action: Rate control for atrial fibrillation: Continue metoprolol, consider digoxin if rate remains >110 bpm despite beta-blocker
expected_management.rationale: New-onset AF is likely precipitant of decompensation, rate control improves diastolic filling

rag_citation.content: Beta-blockers are first-line for rate control in AF with heart failure; digoxin may be added if rate control inadequate

expected_management.action: Anticoagulation for AF: Commence rivaroxaban 20mg daily (NOAC preferred over warfarin given CKD stage 3b, CHA2DS2-VASc score 5)

rag_citation.content: NOACs are preferred over warfarin in AF with CKD stage 3, adjust dose for renal function (rivaroxaban 15mg daily if eGFR 30-49 mL/min)

expected_management.action: Uptitrate ACE inhibitor once euvolaemic (may need to switch to sacubitril/valsartan if EF remains <35% after 3 months)
expected_management.rationale: ARNI therapy reduces mortality in HFrEF more than ACE inhibitors alone

rag_citation.content: Sacubitril/valsartan is superior to ACE inhibitors in reducing cardiovascular mortality in HFrEF (LVEF ≤35%) and should replace ACE inhibitors in stable patients

expected_management.action: Add spironolactone 25mg daily once renal function stabilises (K+ <5.0 mmol/L)
expected_management.rationale: MRA therapy reduces mortality in HFrEF

rag_citation.content: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists reduce mortality in HFrEF (LVEF <35%) and should be added to ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker therapy

expected_management.action: Fluid restriction 1.5L/day, daily weights (alert if >2kg gain in 3 days), low-sodium diet (<2g/day)

rag_citation.content: Fluid restriction to 1.5-2L/day and sodium restriction to <2g/day are recommended for symptomatic heart failure with fluid retention

expected_management.action: Cardiac rehabilitation referral post-discharge, education on medication compliance and symptom recognition
expected_management.rationale: Improve functional capacity and reduce readmissions

rag_citation.content: Multidisciplinary heart failure programs including exercise training reduce hospital readmissions and improve quality of life

expected_management.action: Treat anaemia: Iron studies, consider IV iron if iron deficient (ferritin <100 μg/L or TSAT <20%), target Hb >120 g/L
expected_management.rationale: Anaemia is an independent predictor of poor outcomes in HF

rag_citation.content: Iron deficiency (ferritin <100 μg/L) in heart failure should be treated with IV iron to improve symptoms and exercise capacity

critical_errors.error: Failure to recognise acute decompensated heart failure requiring hospital admission
critical_errors.consequence: Delayed treatment of life-threatening pulmonary oedema, risk of respiratory failure and death
critical_errors.correct_action: Immediate hospital admission for IV diuretics and monitoring

critical_errors.error: Prescribing NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) for chest discomfort without checking fluid status
critical_errors.consequence: Worsening renal function, sodium retention exacerbating fluid overload, increased risk of AKI requiring dialysis
critical_errors.correct_action: Avoid NSAIDs entirely in heart failure and CKD; use paracetamol for analgesia

critical_errors.error: Starting anticoagulation without calculating CHA2DS2-VASc score or assessing bleeding risk (HAS-BLED)
critical_errors.consequence: Inappropriate anticoagulation choice or dosing, increased bleeding risk or inadequate stroke prevention
critical_errors.correct_action: Calculate CHA2DS2-VASc (score 5: age 76, male, CHF, HTN, DM, vascular disease) and HAS-BLED (score 3: age >65, HTN, labile INR if on warfarin) before selecting anticoagulant and dose

critical_errors.error: Failing to adjust NOAC dose for renal function (eGFR 32 mL/min requires rivaroxaban 15mg, not 20mg)
critical_errors.consequence: Increased bleeding risk due to drug accumulation in renal impairment
critical_errors.correct_action: Check eGFR and adjust NOAC dose accordingly (rivaroxaban 15mg daily for eGFR 30-49 mL/min)

critical_errors.error: Discharging patient on oral diuretics without ensuring euvolaemia first
critical_errors.consequence: Early readmission within 30 days due to persistent fluid overload
critical_errors.correct_action: Achieve target weight (return to 87kg baseline) and clinical euvolaemia before discharge

critical_errors.error: Not arranging follow-up echocardiogram to assess LV function after treatment
critical_errors.consequence: Missed opportunity to escalate therapy to sacubitril/valsartan if LVEF remains <35%
critical_errors.correct_action: Arrange repeat echo in 3 months to reassess LVEF and guide further management

fracp_reviews.comments: Excellent case representing typical acute decompensated heart failure presentation in elderly Australian patient. Accurate representation of cardiorenal syndrome and new-onset AF as common precipitants. Management plan aligns with current National Heart Foundation guidelines and eTG recommendations. Appropriate complexity for AMC Clinical Examination medium difficulty.
fracp_reviews.suggested_modifications: None. Case is realistic and well-structured.

fracp_reviews.comments: Clinically accurate case with appropriate Australian context (PBS restrictions, MBS items, eTG citations). Critical errors list is comprehensive and educationally valuable. Social history and functional status assessment align with AMC blueprint requirements. SOCRATES symptom structure is well-implemented.
fracp_reviews.suggested_modifications: None. Case meets all AMC Clinical Examination standards.

learning_objectives: Recognise the clinical presentation of acute decompensated heart failure (NYHA Class IV) with pulmonary oedema requiring urgent hospital admission
Identify new-onset atrial fibrillation as a common precipitant of heart failure decompensation and understand the need for rate control and anticoagulation (CHA2DS2-VASc scoring)
Apply appropriate fluid management strategies in cardiorenal syndrome, balancing diuretic therapy with renal function preservation
Demonstrate knowledge of guideline-directed medical therapy for HFrEF: ACE inhibitor/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor (quadruple therapy)
Adjust anticoagulation dosing for renal impairment (NOAC dose reduction in CKD stage 3b)
Recognise the prognostic significance of anaemia in heart failure and understand iron replacement strategies
Understand the role of NT-proBNP in diagnosing and risk-stratifying acute heart failure
Apply Australian-specific medication access considerations (PBS restrictions for sacubitril/valsartan requiring prior ACE inhibitor failure and LVEF ≤35%)
